title: Try a new case
subtitle: An optional written transfer check after the ten chapters
intro: Use this fictional case to try the ideas on a new problem. Set aside about 20–30 minutes. Answer the five tasks on paper or in a private notes app. Then open the suggested reasoning and compare it with your answers.
paragraphs: A neighborhood garden runs an orientation session. The coordinator gives several spoken instructions while participants inspect seed trays and answer messages. Later, some participants omit a step. The coordinator concludes that they have poor memory.

One tray has a worn handwritten label. Two people read it differently after hearing different suggestions. A participant later recalls seeing a red warning sticker, although the first photograph shows no sticker at that time. Several people had discussed a red sticker after the session.

The team wants participants to explain a planting rule next week. One plan is to reread the same notes several times immediately. Another uses brief explanations from memory, feedback and a delayed revisit with a new example. The coordinator prefers the first plan because it feels easier.

A vivid plant disease is described as the main cause of failed seedlings, but the group has no count of all comparable trays. A proposed change is described as cutting failures by half; the underlying invented rates are four failures in one hundred trays before the change and two in one hundred after it. Weather and seed type also changed.

tasks.title: Separate observation and process
tasks.prompt: Identify two observations and two proposed processes. Give a plausible alternative to the poor-memory explanation. Design a comparison that changes one relevant demand and records a suitable outcome.
tasks.answer: Omitted steps are observations; poor memory is a process claim. Divided attention, instruction ambiguity or a working-memory demand are alternatives. Compare similar tasks with spoken-only versus accurate written instructions, keeping complexity and distractions similar, and record errors and completion time. Random assignment or balanced order can help, while novelty, strategy and practice still require attention.

tasks.title: Interpret the label and later report
tasks.prompt: Explain how sensory input, expectations, question wording and source monitoring might contribute. Write an open question and name an independent record with a limitation.
tasks.answer: The worn strokes provide ambiguous sensory input; suggestions can influence interpretation. Later discussion may supply a sticker detail whose source is misattributed. Ask what the person remembers before introducing a color or object. Compare the early account with a timestamped photograph, while noting its viewpoint and limited time coverage. These are hypotheses, not proof of a false memory or deception.

tasks.title: Choose a learning check
tasks.prompt: Compare the study plans against the goal of explaining a rule next week. Include feedback, a delay, a new example and a confidence–performance comparison.
tasks.answer: Practise an unaided explanation, check it against an accurate reference and revisit after a meaningful delay. A new planting example tests selection and application beyond familiar wording. Record confidence before the explanation and compare it with accuracy across several suitable tasks. The easier immediate experience is not itself evidence of stronger delayed learning.

tasks.title: Test the numerical claim
tasks.prompt: What records are missing for the disease-frequency claim? State the absolute and relative change in the invented rates, then identify a causal limitation and a better comparison.
tasks.answer: Frequency needs a defined reference group and all relevant outcomes, not only memorable failures. Four to two failures per hundred is a two-percentage-point decrease and a fifty-percent relative reduction. Weather and seed type changed too, so the before-and-after difference does not isolate the proposed intervention. Compare comparable trays while varying the intervention appropriately, measure relevant outcomes and retain sampling uncertainty.

tasks.title: Make a bounded recommendation
tasks.prompt: Recommend one practical change and the evidence that would make you keep, revise or abandon it. Avoid claiming a general cognitive improvement from a local task result.
tasks.answer: An accurate checklist could reduce the need to maintain the whole instruction sequence. Predict fewer omitted steps on comparable tasks and check whether the aid remains accessible and current. A helpful local effect supports this design in these conditions; it does not prove that general memory capacity increased. Revise the recommendation if errors persist, new errors emerge or the intended task changes.

rubric.title: Relevant distinctions
rubric.strong: Uses the relevant concepts accurately and separates observations from interpretations.
rubric.developing: Adds labels without explaining what they mean or how they fit the case.

rubric.title: Evidence and alternatives
rubric.strong: Names competing accounts and a comparison or source that could distinguish them.
rubric.developing: Treats a plausible story, score or association as a settled cause.

rubric.title: Limits and application
rubric.strong: Makes a proportionate recommendation and states uncertainty, context and what would change it.
rubric.developing: Generalizes beyond the sample or imposes a fixed conclusion on an individual.

followup: Return tomorrow and again in about a week with a new example. Compare the quality of your reasoning rather than counting pages visited. This self-check does not certify mastery or demonstrate all real-world transfer.
